title: Χρύσεον νέφος
titleEn: The Cloud of Gold and the Fall of Hector — Iliad 14.329–432
part: The Cloud of Gold and the Fall of Hector (14.329–432)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hera objects that the gods could see them on the open peaks of Ida, and Zeus answers that he will wrap them in a golden cloud. He takes her in his arms, the earth sends up flowers beneath them, and he sleeps. Sleep runs to Poseidon and tells him to help the Danaans while Zeus is asleep. Poseidon rallies the Argives, the wounded kings exchange armour so that the best arms go to the best men, and he leads them out with a great sword. Hector marshals the Trojans, and the shout of the two armies is louder than sea, fire or wind. Hector casts at Ajax and fails to wound him; Ajax strikes Hector down with a stone, and he falls like an oak struck by lightning. The Achaeans rush to drag him off, but the Trojan leaders shield him and carry him back to his horses and the city.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ δολοφρονέουσα προσηύδα πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: ton de dolophroneousa prosēuda potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: And to him, with guile in her mind, spoke lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then lady Hera, with guile in her mind, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’: in Homer the article is a pronoun, and the one addressed is Zeus, whose speech of desire closed the last part. δολοφρονέουσα is ‘with guile in her mind’ (δόλος ‘guile’, φρήν ‘mind’), a participle agreeing with Ἥρη. πότνια ‘lady’ is Hera’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: ainotate Kronidē poion ton mython eeipes.
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: Hera’s speech begins as a protest. αἰνότατε is the vocative of the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, and Κρονίδη is the vocative of the patronymic Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’, that is, Zeus. ποῖον … μῦθον is ‘what sort of word’. ἔειπες is the epic aorist of εἶπον (Attic εἶπες), with its first vowel doubled.

sentences.t:
εἰ νῦν ἐν φιλότητι λιλαίεαι εὐνηθῆναι
Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι, τὰ δὲ προπέφανται ἅπαντα·
sentences.tr:
ei nyn en philotēti lilaieai eunēthēnai
Idēs en koryphēisi, ta de propephantai hapanta·
sentences.l:
If now in love you long to lie down
on the peaks of Ida, and all these things are in plain view;
sentences.i: If you long now to lie down in love on the peaks of Ida, and yet everything lies in plain view;
sentences.n: Hera raises her objection. λιλαίεαι is the present of λιλαίομαι ‘long for’, with the infinitive εὐνηθῆναι, the aorist passive of εὐνάζω ‘put to bed’, here in a middle sense, ‘to lie down’. ἐν φιλότητι is ‘in love’. Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι is ‘on the peaks of Ida’ (Ida is the mountain above Troy), with the epic dative plural -ῃσι. τά is ‘these things’, and προπέφανται, a perfect passive of προφαίνω, says they have been brought into view.

sentences.l:
how would it be, if some one of the gods, the forever-born, us two
sleeping should catch sight of, and among all the gods going
should tell it?
sentences.i: How would it be if one of the everlasting gods should catch sight of the two of us asleep, and go among all the gods and tell it?
sentences.n: κ’ ἔοι is κε ἔοι, the epic optative of εἰμί (Attic εἴη): ‘how would it be?’. The condition is εἰ … ἀθρήσειε … πεφράδοι, two aorist optatives, ‘if one should see … and tell’. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, and εὕδοντ’ is an elided participle, ‘sleeping’, agreeing with νῶϊ. θεῶν αἰειγενετάων is ‘of the gods, the forever-born’, a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way. μετελθών is ‘going among’, and πεφράδοι, from φράζω ‘point out, tell’, has no object in the Greek: ‘it’ is understood.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγε τεὸν πρὸς δῶμα νεοίμην
ἐξ εὐνῆς ἀνστᾶσα, νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη.
sentences.tr:
ouk an egōge teon pros dōma neoimēn
ex eunēs anstasa, nemessēton de ken eiē.
sentences.l:
I for my part would not go to your house
rising from the bed; and it would be a thing to resent.
sentences.i: I, for my part, would not go to your house after rising from the bed; that would be a thing to resent.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν … νεοίμην is ‘I would not go’: νεοίμην is the optative of νέομαι ‘go, go back’, and ἔγωγε is the emphatic ‘I for one’. τεὸν is the epic form of σόν ‘your’, so the house is Zeus’s. ἀνστᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, ‘having risen’. νεμεσσητόν is ‘a thing to be resented’ (from νεμεσσάω), and κεν εἴη is a potential optative, ‘it would be’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δή ῥ’ ἐθέλεις καί τοι φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ,
ἔστιν τοι θάλαμος, τόν τοι φίλος υἱὸς ἔτευξεν
Ἥφαιστος, πυκινὰς δὲ θύρας σταθμοῖσιν ἐπῆρσεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ei dē rh’ etheleis kai toi philon epleto thymōi,
estin toi thalamos, ton toi philos huios eteuxen
Hēphaistos, pykinas de thyras stathmoisin epērsen·
sentences.i: But if you truly wish it, and it is dear to your heart, there is a chamber that your dear son Hephaestus made for you, and he fitted close-fitting doors to its doorposts;
sentences.n: The main clause is ἔστιν τοι θάλαμος, ‘there is a chamber for you’; everything before it is the condition ‘if you truly wish it’. τοι is the epic ‘for you’ (= σοι) and appears three times. φίλος υἱός ‘dear son’ is Hephaestus, who is named in apposition at the start of the last line. ἔπλετο is ‘has come to be’. πυκινάς, here ‘close-fitting’ (the word’s sense is ‘close, compact’), describes the doors, and ἐπῆρσεν, from ἐπαραρίσκω, is ‘fitted’; σταθμοῖσιν is ‘to the doorposts’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἴομεν κείοντες, ἐπεί νύ τοι εὔαδεν εὐνή.
sentences.tr: enth’ iomen keiontes, epei ny toi euaden eunē.
sentences.l: There let us go to lie down, since now the bed has pleased you.”
sentences.i: Let us go there to lie down, since the bed is to your liking.”
sentences.n: ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive used as an exhortation, ‘let us go’. κείοντες is a participle of κείω ‘wish to lie down’, the desiderative of κεῖμαι, so ‘to lie down’ is its purpose. εὔαδεν is the epic aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, and εὐνή is ‘bed’. This ends Hera’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’ (Hera) and ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, the usual opening of a reply. νεφεληγερέτα ‘cloud-gatherer’, with the epic nominative in -α, is Zeus’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way; it suits the cloud he is about to spread.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη μήτε θεῶν τό γε δείδιθι μήτέ τιν’ ἀνδρῶν
ὄψεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Hērē mēte theōn to ge deidithi mēte tin’ andrōn
opsesthai·
sentences.l:
“Hera, neither fear this of the gods, nor that any of men
will see;
sentences.i: “Hera, do not fear that any of the gods will see, or any of men;
sentences.n: δείδιθι is the perfect imperative of δείδω ‘fear’, with present sense. τό γε ‘this’ looks forward to the infinitive ὄψεσθαι, the future infinitive of ὁράω ‘see’, so the fear is ‘that anyone will see’. μήτε θεῶν μήτε τιν’ ἀνδρῶν is ‘neither (anyone) of gods nor any of men’, and the Greek gives ὄψεσθαι no object.

sentences.t:
τοῖόν τοι ἐγὼ νέφος ἀμφικαλύψω
χρύσεον·
sentences.tr:
toion toi egō nephos amphikalypsō
chryseon·
sentences.l:
such a cloud I will enfold about you,
golden;
sentences.i: I will enfold you in such a cloud, a golden one;
sentences.n: τοῖον ‘such’ looks ahead to the next unit, where the cloud is described by what it does. ἀμφικαλύψω is the future of ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘enfold’ (literally ‘cover round’), and τοι is ‘for you’ (= σοι). χρύσεον, ‘golden’, is the uncontracted form of Attic χρυσοῦν.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν νῶϊ διαδράκοι Ἠέλιός περ,
οὗ τε καὶ ὀξύτατον πέλεται φάος εἰσοράασθαι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an nōï diadrakoi Ēelios per,
hou te kai oxytaton peletai phaos eisoraasthai.
sentences.l:
nor could even the Sun see through to us two,
whose light too is sharpest for looking.”
sentences.i: and not even the Sun could see through it to the two of us, he whose light is sharpest for looking.”
sentences.n: διαδράκοι is the aorist optative of διαδέρκομαι ‘see through’, and with ἄν it says what the Sun could not do. Ἠέλιός περ is ‘even the Sun’. οὗ τε is ‘whose’, with epic τε. φάος εἰσοράασθαι, ‘light for looking’, can be taken either of the Sun’s light as the keenest to see by or as the keenest to look at, and the English keeps the Greek’s wording. This ends Zeus’s speech.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀγκὰς ἔμαρπτε Κρόνου παῖς ἣν παράκοιτιν·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai ankas emarpte Kronou pais hēn parakoitin·
sentences.l: He spoke, and in his arms the son of Cronus seized his own consort;
sentences.i: So he said, and the son of Cronus seized his wife in his arms;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καὶ is ‘he spoke, and’. ἀγκάς ‘in the arms’ goes with ἔμαρπτε, imperfect of μάρπτω ‘seize’. Κρόνου παῖς is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus, and ἣν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative; παράκοιτις is ‘consort’, a wife who lies beside her husband.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ὑπὸ χθὼν δῖα φύεν νεοθηλέα ποίην,
λωτόν θ’ ἑρσήεντα ἰδὲ κρόκον ἠδ’ ὑάκινθον
πυκνὸν καὶ μαλακόν, ὃς ἀπὸ χθονὸς ὑψόσ’ ἔεργε.
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ hypo chthōn dia phyen neothēlea poiēn,
lōton th’ hersēenta ide krokon ēd’ hyakinthon
pyknon kai malakon, hos apo chthonos hypsos’ eerge.
sentences.l:
and beneath them the heavenly earth made grow new-sprouting grass,
and dewy lotus and crocus and hyacinth,
thick and soft, which up from the ground kept them aloft.
sentences.i: Beneath them the heavenly earth made newly sprouting grass grow, and dewy lotus, and crocus and hyacinth, thick and soft, which kept them high above the ground.
sentences.n: φύεν is the unaugmented imperfect of φύω used causatively, ‘made grow’, and χθὼν δῖα is ‘the heavenly earth’. νεοθηλέα ‘new-sprouting’ is from νέος ‘new’ and θάλλω ‘bloom’. λωτός is a clover-like fodder plant; what ὑάκινθος was is not certain. The relative ὅς agrees with ὑάκινθον, the last-named, but what holds the two of them up is the whole thick growth; the Greek does not say whom it holds up, and ‘them’ is Zeus and Hera.

sentences.t:
τῷ ἔνι λεξάσθην, ἐπὶ δὲ νεφέλην ἕσσαντο
καλὴν χρυσείην·
sentences.tr:
tōi eni lexasthēn, epi de nephelēn hessanto
kalēn chryseiēn·
sentences.l:
In that the two laid themselves down, and over themselves put on a cloud,
beautiful, golden;
sentences.i: The two lay down in it and put a beautiful golden cloud on over themselves;
sentences.n: τῷ ἔνι is ‘in it’, the flowery bed. λεξάσθην is a dual aorist middle of λέγω ‘lay down’, ‘the two laid themselves down’. ἕσσαντο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, so the two ‘clothed themselves’ with the cloud, and ἐπί is an adverb, ‘on over’. χρυσείην is another form of ‘golden’ (compare χρύσεον above).

sentences.t: στιλπναὶ δ’ ἀπέπιπτον ἔερσαι.
sentences.tr: stilpnai d’ apepipton eersai.
sentences.l: and glistening dews fell away.
sentences.i: and glistening drops of dew fell from it.
sentences.n: ἔερσαι is the plural of ἐέρση ‘dew’, here drops of dew, and στιλπναί ‘glistening’ describes them. ἀπέπιπτον is the imperfect of ἀποπίπτω ‘fall off’; the ἀπο- gives ‘from it’, the cloud.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ μὲν ἀτρέμας εὗδε πατὴρ ἀνὰ Γαργάρῳ ἄκρῳ,
ὕπνῳ καὶ φιλότητι δαμείς, ἔχε δ’ ἀγκὰς ἄκοιτιν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men atremas heude patēr ana Gargarōi akrōi,
hypnōi kai philotēti dameis, eche d’ ankas akoitin·
sentences.l:
So he, for his part, motionless slept, the father, on topmost Gargarus,
overcome by sleep and love, and held in his arms his wife;
sentences.i: So the father, for his part, slept motionless on the peak of Gargarus, overcome by sleep and love, and held his wife in his arms;
sentences.n: Zeus is not named but called πατήρ ‘the father’; his name comes in Sleep’s speech. ἀνὰ Γαργάρῳ ἄκρῳ is ‘on topmost Gargarus’, the summit of Ida, ἀνά with the dative in the epic way. ἀτρέμας is ‘motionless’. δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overpower’, and ἔχε … ἀγκὰς ἄκοιτιν is ‘held his wife in his arms’. ὃ μὲν sets Zeus against Sleep in the next unit.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ θέειν ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν νήδυμος Ὕπνος
ἀγγελίην ἐρέων γαιηόχῳ ἐννοσιγαίῳ·
sentences.tr:
bē de theein epi nēas Achaiōn nēdymos Hypnos
angeliēn ereōn gaiēochōi ennosigaiōi·
sentences.l:
and he went to run to the ships of the Achaeans, sweet Sleep,
news to tell to the earth-holder, the earth-shaker;
sentences.i: and sweet Sleep set off running to the ships of the Achaeans to tell the news to the earth-holder, the earth-shaker;
sentences.n: βῆ δὲ θέειν is ‘he went to run’, that is, ‘set off running’; θέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of θέω. ἐρέων is a future participle of ἐρέω ‘say, tell’, expressing purpose. νήδυμος ‘sweet’ is Sleep’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way, and its meaning and origin are not known. γαιηόχῳ ἐννοσιγαίῳ ‘earth-holder, earth-shaker’ are Poseidon’s epithets used without his name, which comes in the next speech.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ is ‘close by’, and ἱστάμενος the present middle participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is a formula for words that are spoken and fly to the hearer; the Greek calls them ‘winged’ whatever they say. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
πρόφρων νῦν Δαναοῖσι Ποσείδαον ἐπάμυνε,
καί σφιν κῦδος ὄπαζε μίνυνθά περ, ὄφρ’ ἔτι εὕδει
Ζεύς, ἐπεὶ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμ’ ἐκάλυψα·
sentences.tr:
prophrōn nyn Danaoisi Poseidaon epamyne,
kai sphin kydos opaze minyntha per, ophr’ eti heudei
Zeus, epei autōi egō malakon peri kōm’ ekalypsa·
sentences.i: “Now, Poseidon, come to the defence of the Danaans with a ready mind, and grant them glory, if only for a little while, so long as Zeus still sleeps, since I have covered him round with soft slumber;
sentences.n: Sleep’s speech. πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’, and ἐπάμυνε the imperative of ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence of’, with the dative Δαναοῖσι, and Ποσείδαον is the vocative of Ποσειδάων. ὄπαζε is the imperative of ὀπάζω ‘grant’. μίνυνθά περ is ‘for a little while at least’. ὄφρ’ ἔτι εὕδει is ‘while he still sleeps’, εὕδει being the present of εὕδω. κῶμα is deep sleep, ‘slumber’. ἐκάλυψα is the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t: Ἥρη δ’ ἐν φιλότητι παρήπαφεν εὐνηθῆναι.
sentences.tr: Hērē d’ en philotēti parēpaphen eunēthēnai.
sentences.l: and Hera in love has beguiled him to lie down.”
sentences.i: and Hera, in love, has beguiled him into lying down.”
sentences.n: Ἥρη is the subject: it is Hera who has beguiled (παρήπαφεν, a reduplicated aorist of ἀπαφίσκω with the prefix παρα-) Zeus, and εὐνηθῆναι, the aorist passive infinitive of εὐνάζω, says what she has brought him to do, ‘to lie down’. ἐν φιλότητι ‘in love’ can go with the beguiling or with the lying down, and the English keeps it between the two. This ends Sleep’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν ᾤχετ’ ἐπὶ κλυτὰ φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων,
τὸν δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀνῆκεν ἀμυνέμεναι Δαναοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn ho men ōichet’ epi klyta phyl’ anthrōpōn,
ton d’ eti mallon anēken amynemenai Danaoisin.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he went off to the famous tribes of men,
and him still more he urged on to defend the Danaans.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went off to the famous tribes of men, and urged him on still more to defend the Danaans.
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν is Sleep, who goes off, and τὸν, ‘him’, is Poseidon, the one he rouses. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone, go off’. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘send up, urge on’, and ἀμυνέμεναι the epic infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, which with the dative of a person (here Δαναοῖσιν) means ‘defend’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἐν πρώτοισι μέγα προθορὼν ἐκέλευσεν·
sentences.tr: autika d’ en prōtoisi mega prothorōn ekeleusen·
sentences.l: At once among the first, greatly leaping forward, he bade:
sentences.i: At once he leapt far forward among the foremost and bade them:
sentences.n: The subject is Poseidon, who now acts on Sleep’s urging. ἐν πρώτοισι is ‘among the first’, the foremost fighters. προθορών is the aorist participle of προθρῴσκω ‘leap forward’, and μέγα here is ‘greatly, far’. ἐκέλευσεν is the aorist of κελεύω ‘bid’, and what he bids follows.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι καὶ δ’ αὖτε μεθίεμεν Ἕκτορι νίκην
Πριαμίδῃ, ἵνα νῆας ἕλῃ καὶ κῦδος ἄρηται;
sentences.tr:
Argeioi kai d’ aute methiemen Hektori nikēn
Priamidēi, hina nēas helēi kai kydos arētai;
sentences.l:
“Argives, and further, again, are we to let go the victory to Hector,
Priam’s-son, so that he may take the ships and win glory?
sentences.i: “Argives, are we, once again, to hand the victory over to Hector, son of Priam, so that he may take the ships and win glory?
sentences.n: Poseidon’s speech, a question of reproach. μεθίεμεν is the epic infinitive in -μεν of μεθίημι ‘let go’, and an infinitive can ask ‘are we to …?’; here it has two objects, νίκην ‘victory’ and the dative Ἕκτορι, ‘let go to Hector’. Πριαμίδῃ is the dative of the patronymic ‘son of Priam’. ἕλῃ and ἄρηται are aorist subjunctives after ἵνα, ‘that he may take’ and ‘may win’ (ἄρηται is from ἄρνυμαι).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν οὕτω φησὶ καὶ εὔχεται οὕνεκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσι μένει κεχολωμένος ἦτορ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men houtō phēsi kai euchetai hounek’ Achilleus
nēusin epi glaphyrēisi menei kecholōmenos ētor·
sentences.l:
But he says so and vaunts, because Achilles
by the hollow ships stays, angered in heart;
sentences.i: But Hector speaks and boasts like this because Achilles stays by the hollow ships, angered at heart;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν is Hector, the man named just before, and οὕτω φησὶ καὶ εὔχεται is ‘says so and vaunts’. οὕνεκ’ is ‘because’, and the reason is Achilles’ absence from the fighting. νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσι is ‘by the hollow ships’, with the epic dative plural -ῃσι. κεχολωμένος is the perfect participle of χολόω ‘anger’, and ἦτορ ‘heart’ is an accusative of respect: angered ‘in the heart’.

sentences.t:
κείνου δ’ οὔ τι λίην ποθὴ ἔσσεται, εἴ κεν οἳ ἄλλοι
ἡμεῖς ὀτρυνώμεθ’ ἀμυνέμεν ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.tr:
keinou d’ ou ti liēn pothē essetai, ei ken hoi alloi
hēmeis otrynōmeth’ amynemen allēloisin.
sentences.l:
and of him there will be no very great lack, if we, the others,
urge ourselves on to defend one another.
sentences.i: and there will be no great lack of him if the rest of us urge one another on to defend each other.
sentences.n: ποθή is ‘lack’, the sense of being without someone, and οὔ τι λίην is ‘not at all very’, so ‘no very great lack’. κείνου is the Ionic form of ἐκείνου ‘of him’ (Achilles). εἴ κεν with the subjunctive ὀτρυνώμεθ’ is ‘if we urge’, the middle ‘urge ourselves, each other’. ἀμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, which with a dative of the person means ‘defend’, and ἀλλήλοισιν ‘one another’ is that dative.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.tr: all’ ageth’ hōs an egō eipō peithōmetha pantes·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: ἄγεθ’ is the imperative ἄγετε ‘come on’. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω is ‘as I shall say’, an ἄν with the aorist subjunctive, and πειθώμεθα is the subjunctive ‘let us obey’.

sentences.t:
ἀσπίδες ὅσσαι ἄρισται ἐνὶ στρατῷ ἠδὲ μέγισται
ἑσσάμενοι, κεφαλὰς δὲ παναίθῃσιν κορύθεσσι
κρύψαντες, χερσίν τε τὰ μακρότατ’ ἔγχε’ ἑλόντες
ἴομεν·
sentences.tr:
aspides hossai aristai eni stratōi ēde megistai
hessamenoi, kephalas de panaithēisin korythessi
krypsantes, chersin te ta makrotat’ enche’ helontes
iomen·
sentences.l:
The shields that are best in the army and greatest
having put on, and our heads with all-blazing helmets
having hidden, and in our hands the longest spears
having taken, let us go;
sentences.i: Let us put on the best and biggest shields in the army, cover our heads with blazing helmets, take the longest spears in our hands, and go;
sentences.n: One long sentence built on three aorist participles, ἑσσάμενοι ‘having put on’, κρύψαντες ‘having hidden’ and ἑλόντες ‘having taken’, all waiting for the verb ἴομεν ‘let us go’. ἄρισται and μέγισται are superlatives ‘best’ and ‘greatest’. παναίθῃσιν, ‘all-blazing’ (πᾶν + αἴθω ‘burn’), qualifies the helmets, and ἔγχε’ is the elided ἔγχεα ‘spears’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἡγήσομαι, οὐδ’ ἔτι φημὶ
Ἕκτορα Πριαμίδην μενέειν μάλα περ μεμαῶτα.
sentences.tr:
autar egōn hēgēsomai, oud’ eti phēmi
Hektora Priamidēn meneein mala per memaōta.
sentences.l:
and I will lead, and I no longer say
that Hector, Priam’s-son, will stand firm, though he is very eager.
sentences.i: and I will lead the way; and I no longer think that Hector, son of Priam, will stand his ground, however eager he may be.
sentences.n: ἡγήσομαι is the future of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, and φημί here is ‘say, think’. μενέειν is the future infinitive of μένω ‘stand fast, withstand’ (the attackers understood). μάλα περ μεμαῶτα, ‘though very eager’, is the perfect participle of μέμαα, agreeing with Ἕκτορα. Πριαμίδην is the patronymic ‘son of Priam’ again.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνὴρ μενέχαρμος, ἔχει δ’ ὀλίγον σάκος ὤμῳ,
χείρονι φωτὶ δότω, ὃ δ’ ἐν ἀσπίδι μείζονι δύτω.
sentences.tr:
hos de k’ anēr menecharmos, echei d’ oligon sakos ōmōi,
cheironi phōti dotō, ho d’ en aspidi meizoni dytō.
sentences.l:
And whoever is a man steadfast in the fight, and has a small shield on his shoulder,
to a worse man let him give it, and himself in a bigger shield let him get inside.”
sentences.i: And let any man who is steadfast in battle but carries a small shield on his shoulder give it to a worse man, and himself get into a bigger shield.”
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνὴρ μενέχαρμος is ‘whoever is a man steadfast in the fight’, with ‘is’ left out, and it is followed by two imperatives, δότω ‘let him give’ and δύτω ‘let him get into’. μενέχαρμος is ‘steadfast in the fight’ (μένω ‘stand fast’ + χάρμη ‘battle’). σάκος and ἀσπίς both mean ‘shield’. χείρονι φωτί is ‘to a worse man’. This ends Poseidon’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēde pithonto·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’. τοῦ is the genitive ‘him’ after κλύον, which is an unaugmented aorist of κλύω ‘hear, listen to’; πίθοντο is the aorist of πείθομαι ‘obey’. μάλα is ‘readily’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ αὐτοὶ βασιλῆες ἐκόσμεον οὐτάμενοί περ
Τυδεΐδης Ὀδυσεύς τε καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ autoi basilēes ekosmeon outamenoi per
Tydeïdēs Odyseus te kai Atreïdēs Agamemnōn·
sentences.l:
And them the kings themselves set in order, though wounded,
Tydeus’-son and Odysseus and Atreus’-son Agamemnon;
sentences.i: And the kings themselves, though wounded, marshalled them: the son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, son of Atreus;
sentences.n: τοὺς is ‘them’, the army that has just obeyed. αὐτοὶ βασιλῆες ‘the kings themselves’ are named in the second line; they are wounded, as in the scene earlier in this book where they came up from the ships. ἐκόσμεον is the uncontracted imperfect of κοσμέω ‘set in order’, and οὐτάμενοί περ is ‘though wounded’. Τυδεΐδης and Ἀτρεΐδης are patronymics, ‘son of Tydeus’ and ‘son of Atreus’.

sentences.t: οἰχόμενοι δ’ ἐπὶ πάντας ἀρήϊα τεύχε’ ἄμειβον·
sentences.tr: oichomenoi d’ epi pantas arēïa teuche’ ameibon·
sentences.l: and going to all, warlike armour they exchanged;
sentences.i: and going about to all of them, they exchanged the warlike armour;
sentences.n: οἰχόμενοι, from οἴχομαι, is ‘going’, here going about. ἐπὶ πάντας is ‘to all’. ἀρήϊα τεύχεα is ‘warlike armour’ (ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’), and ἄμειβον is the imperfect of ἀμείβω ‘exchange’.

sentences.t: ἐσθλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὸς ἔδυνε, χέρεια δὲ χείρονι δόσκεν.
sentences.tr: esthla men esthlos edyne, chereia de cheironi dosken.
sentences.l: good things the good man put on, and worse things to the worse man he gave.
sentences.i: The good man put on the good armour, and gave the worse armour to the worse man.
sentences.n: The lines say what the exchange was: ἐσθλά ‘good things’ (the good armour) go to ἐσθλός ‘the good man’, χέρεια ‘worse things’ to χείρονι ‘the worse man’. ἔδυνε is the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’, and δόσκεν is an iterative imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘used to give’, so the sentence describes what each man did each time.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἕσσαντο περὶ χροῒ νώροπα χαλκὸν
βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ hessanto peri chroï nōropa chalkon
ban rh’ imen·
sentences.l:
But when they had put on about their skin the flashing bronze,
they set off to go;
sentences.i: But when they had put the flashing bronze about their bodies, they set out;
sentences.n: ἕσσαντο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘put on’, and περὶ χροΐ is ‘about the skin’. νώροπα, ‘flashing’, is the traditional gloss; the word’s meaning is not known. βάν is the unaugmented aorist ‘they went’ (= ἔβησαν), and ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι: ‘they set out to go’.

sentences.t:
ἦρχε δ’ ἄρά σφι Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
δεινὸν ἄορ τανύηκες ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ παχείῃ
εἴκελον ἀστεροπῇ·
sentences.tr:
ērche d’ ara sphi Poseidaōn enosichthōn
deinon aor tanyēkes echōn en cheiri pacheiēi
eikelon asteropēi·
sentences.i: and Poseidon the earth-shaker led them, holding in his stout hand a dread, long-pointed sword, like lightning;
sentences.n: ἦρχε is ‘led’ and takes the dative σφι ‘them’. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘Poseidon earth-shaker’, translated as always. τανύηκες is ‘long-pointed’ (the second part usually taken as ‘point, edge’, not certain), and ἄορ is ‘sword’. παχείῃ, ‘stout’ (literally ‘thick’), agrees with χειρί. εἴκελον ἀστεροπῇ is ‘like lightning’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ οὐ θέμις ἐστὶ μιγῆναι
ἐν δαῒ λευγαλέῃ, ἀλλὰ δέος ἰσχάνει ἄνδρας.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ou themis esti migēnai
en daï leugaleēi, alla deos ischanei andras.
sentences.l:
and with it it is not right to be mingled
in pitiful battle, but fear holds men back.
sentences.i: It is not right to meet it in pitiful battle, but fear holds men back.
sentences.n: τῷ most naturally means ‘with it’, the sword, though ‘with him’, Poseidon, is possible. οὐ θέμις ἐστί is ‘it is not right’, and μιγῆναι the aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι, ‘to be mingled with’, that is, to meet in battle. δαΐ is the dative of δαΐς ‘battle’, and λευγαλέῃ ‘pitiful’. ἰσχάνει is ‘holds back’.

sentences.t: Τρῶας δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκόσμει φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr: Trōas d’ auth’ heterōthen ekosmei phaidimos Hektōr.
sentences.l: And the Trojans, in turn, from the other side, glorious Hector set in order.
sentences.i: On the other side glorious Hector, in his turn, marshalled the Trojans.
sentences.n: The nominative is φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ, ‘glorious Hector’, and Τρῶας is the object, though the Greek puts the object first. αὖθ’ ‘in turn’ and ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ set Hector against Poseidon. ἐκόσμει is the imperfect of κοσμέω ‘set in order’, as in the line about the kings. φαίδιμος is the stock epithet of Hector, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
δή ῥα τότ’ αἰνοτάτην ἔριδα πτολέμοιο τάνυσσαν
κυανοχαῖτα Ποσειδάων καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ,
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν Τρώεσσιν, ὃ δ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἀρήγων.
sentences.tr:
dē rha tot’ ainotatēn erida ptolemoio tanyssan
kyanochaita Poseidaōn kai phaidimos Hektōr,
ētoi ho men Trōessin, ho d’ Argeioisin arēgōn.
sentences.l:
Then indeed the most dread strife of war they stretched,
dark-haired Poseidon and glorious Hector,
the one helping the Trojans, the other the Argives.
sentences.i: Then, indeed, dark-haired Poseidon and glorious Hector stretched out the most dreadful strife of war, the one helping the Trojans, the other the Argives.
sentences.n: The two subjects are κυανοχαῖτα Ποσειδάων and φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ; κυανοχαῖτα, ‘dark-haired’ (κυανός ‘dark’ + χαίτη ‘hair’), has the epic nominative in -α. τάνυσσαν is the aorist of τανύω ‘stretch’: the picture is usually taken to be a rope stretched tight between the two sides. αἰνοτάτην is the superlative ‘most dread’. ἤτοι ὃ μὲν … ὃ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’, and ἀρήγων ‘helping’ takes the dative.

sentences.t:
ἐκλύσθη δὲ θάλασσα ποτὶ κλισίας τε νέας τε
Ἀργείων· οἳ δὲ ξύνισαν μεγάλῳ ἀλαλητῷ.
sentences.tr:
eklysthē de thalassa poti klisias te neas te
Argeiōn· hoi de xynisan megalōi alalētōi.
sentences.l:
And the sea was washed up in a surge toward the huts and the ships
of the Argives; and they brought themselves together with a great outcry.
sentences.i: And the sea surged up toward the huts and the ships of the Argives; and the armies met with a great outcry.
sentences.n: ἐκλύσθη is the aorist passive of ἐκλύζω ‘wash up, surge up’. κλισίας are the army’s ‘huts’, and ποτί is the epic form of πρός. οἳ δὲ ξύνισαν is ‘and they met’: ξύνισαν is from ξυνίημι, the old form of συνίημι, ‘bring together’, here intransitive in sense (the same verb stands in ξυνέηκε at 1.8). ἀλαλητός is the shout of battle.

sentences.t:
οὔτε θαλάσσης κῦμα τόσον βοάᾳ ποτὶ χέρσον
ποντόθεν ὀρνύμενον πνοιῇ Βορέω ἀλεγεινῇ·
sentences.tr:
oute thalassēs kyma toson boaāi poti cherson
pontothen ornymenon pnoiēi Boreō alegeinēi·
sentences.l:
Neither does the wave of the sea roar so greatly toward the dry land,
rising from the deep sea by the grievous breath of the North Wind;
sentences.i: Neither does the wave of the sea roar so loudly against the dry land, rising from the deep under the grievous breath of the North Wind;
sentences.n: A comparison of sounds begins, built on οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτε, ‘neither … nor … nor’, and it is finished only at 400 with ὅσση, ‘as great as’. τόσον βοάᾳ is ‘roars so greatly’ (βοάᾳ is βοᾷ with the vowels opened out). ποντόθεν is ‘from the sea’, with -θεν ‘from’. ὀρνύμενον is the present middle participle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’, and Βορέω is the genitive of Βορέης, the North Wind.

sentences.t:
οὔτε πυρὸς τόσσός γε ποτὶ βρόμος αἰθομένοιο
οὔρεος ἐν βήσσῃς, ὅτε τ’ ὤρετο καιέμεν ὕλην·
sentences.tr:
oute pyros tossos ge poti bromos aithomenoio
oureos en bēssēis, hote t’ ōreto kaiemen hylēn·
sentences.l:
nor of blazing fire is the roar so great
in the glens of a mountain, when it has risen to burn the forest;
sentences.i: nor is the roar of blazing fire so loud in the glens of a mountain, when it has risen to burn the forest;
sentences.n: The second term of the comparison: τόσσος … βρόμος is ‘so great a roar’, and αἰθομένοιο is ‘of blazing’ fire. ποτί is an adverb here, ‘besides’, and the English leaves it out. βήσσῃς is a dative plural, ‘in the glens’, with the epic ending -ῃς (= -αις). ὤρετο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rose’, and καιέμεν the epic infinitive of καίω ‘burn’.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ ἄνεμος τόσσόν γε περὶ δρυσὶν ὑψικόμοισι
ἠπύει, ὅς τε μάλιστα μέγα βρέμεται χαλεπαίνων,
ὅσση ἄρα Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ἔπλετο φωνὴ
δεινὸν ἀϋσάντων, ὅτ’ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ὄρουσαν.
sentences.tr:
out’ anemos tosson ge peri drysin hypsikomoisi
ēpyei, hos te malista mega bremetai chalepainōn,
hossē ara Trōōn kai Achaiōn epleto phōnē
deinon aÿsantōn, hot’ ep’ allēloisin orousan.
sentences.l:
nor does the wind so greatly around the high-crowned oaks
cry aloud, which roars most loudly growing harsh,
as great as was the voice of Trojans and Achaeans
shouting fearsomely, when they rushed upon one another.
sentences.i: nor does the wind cry aloud so loudly around the high-crowned oaks, when it roars at its loudest in its fury, as great as was the voice of the Trojans and Achaeans, shouting fearsomely, when they rushed upon one another.
sentences.n: The third term, and then the thing compared: τόσσον … ἠπύει, ‘cries aloud so greatly’, from ἠπύω, is answered by ὅσση ἄρα … φωνή, ‘as great as the voice’, of the two armies. ὑψικόμοισι δρυσί is ‘high-crowned oaks’. ὅς τε is ‘which’, the wind, and χαλεπαίνων is ‘growing harsh’, in a rage. δεινὸν ἀϋσάντων is ‘shouting fearsomely’, a participle agreeing with the genitives Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν. ὄρουσαν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rushed’.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντος δὲ πρῶτος ἀκόντισε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἔγχει, ἐπεὶ τέτραπτο πρὸς ἰθύ οἱ, οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε,
τῇ ῥα δύω τελαμῶνε περὶ στήθεσσι τετάσθην,
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν σάκεος, ὃ δὲ φασγάνου ἀργυροήλου·
sentences.tr:
Aiantos de prōtos akontise phaidimos Hektōr
enchei, epei tetrapto pros ithy hoi, oud’ aphamarte,
tēi rha dyō telamōne peri stēthessi tetasthēn,
ētoi ho men sakeos, ho de phasganou argyroēlou·
sentences.l:
And at Ajax first cast glorious Hector
with his spear, since toward him he was turned straight, and he did not miss,
where the two straps across the chest were stretched,
the one of the shield, the other of the silver-studded sword;
sentences.i: Hector was first to cast his spear at Ajax, for Ajax had turned straight toward him, and he did not miss, at the place where the two straps were stretched across his chest, the one of the shield, the other of the silver-studded sword;
sentences.n: Αἴαντος is the genitive of the target after ἀκόντισε, ‘cast at’, and ἔγχει ‘with the spear’ is dative. τέτραπτο is a pluperfect passive of τρέπω: Ajax ‘had turned’ to face him, and οἱ is ‘him’, Hector. τελαμῶνε and τετάσθην are duals, ‘the two straps’ and ‘were stretched’ (the straps are the shield-sling and the sword-sling); ἀργυροήλου ‘silver-studded’ is from ἦλος ‘nail, stud’.

sentences.t: τώ οἱ ῥυσάσθην τέρενα χρόα.
sentences.tr: tō hoi rhysasthēn terena chroa.
sentences.l: The two of them protected for him the tender skin.
sentences.i: The two straps protected his tender skin.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual ‘the two’ (the two straps), and ῥυσάσθην the dual aorist middle of ῥύομαι ‘protect’. οἱ is ‘for him’. τέρενα, the epic form of τέρεινα, is ‘tender’, and χρόα ‘skin’; so the spear did not draw blood.

sentences.t:
χώσατο δ’ Ἕκτωρ,
ὅττί ῥά οἱ βέλος ὠκὺ ἐτώσιον ἔκφυγε χειρός,
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων.
sentences.tr:
chōsato d’ Hektōr,
hotti rha hoi belos ōky etōsion ekphyge cheiros,
aps d’ hetarōn eis ethnos echazeto kēr’ aleeinōn.
sentences.l:
And Hector was incensed
that for him the swift shaft in vain had flown from his hand,
and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding.
sentences.i: And Hector was incensed that his swift shaft had flown from his hand in vain, and he drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death.
sentences.n: χώσατο is the aorist of χώομαι ‘be incensed’. ὅττί ῥά is ‘that’, giving the reason, and οἱ ‘for him’ is dative. βέλος ὠκύ is ‘a swift shaft’, the spear, and ἐτώσιον ‘in vain’. The last line is the formula ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων; here κῆρ’ is the elided κῆρα, ‘death-fate’, not κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀπιόντα μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
χερμαδίῳ, τά ῥα πολλὰ θοάων ἔχματα νηῶν
πὰρ ποσὶ μαρναμένων ἐκυλίνδετο, τῶν ἓν ἀείρας
στῆθος βεβλήκει ὑπὲρ ἄντυγος ἀγχόθι δειρῆς,
στρόμβον δ’ ὣς ἔσσευε βαλών, περὶ δ’ ἔδραμε πάντῃ.
sentences.tr:
ton men epeit’ apionta megas Telamōnios Aias
chermadiōi, ta rha polla thoaōn echmata nēōn
par posi marnamenōn ekylindeto, tōn hen aeiras
stēthos beblēkei hyper antygos anchothi deirēs,
strombon d’ hōs esseue balōn, peri d’ edrame pantēi.
sentences.l:
Him then as he went away, great Telamonian Ajax
with a stone — which, many of them, supports of the swift ships,
by the feet of the fighters were rolling about — one of them having lifted,
had struck him on the chest above the rim, near the neck,
and like a top he set him whirling, having struck, and around he ran everywhere.
sentences.i: Then, as Hector was going away, great Telamonian Ajax lifted one of the many stones that were rolling about by the feet of the fighters, supports of the swift ships, and with it struck him on the chest above the rim of his shield, close to the neck, and by that blow set him spinning like a top; and he ran round and round in every direction.
sentences.n: The sentence runs through both halves: τὸν is Hector, ἀπιόντα ‘going away’ agrees with him, and χερμαδίῳ is ‘with a stone’. τά ῥα πολλά ‘of which many’ points to the stones lying about; ἔχματα are ‘supports’, the stones that held the beached ships steady (from ἔχω ‘hold’). ἐκυλίνδετο is an imperfect passive ‘were rolling about’, and ἀείρας ‘having lifted’ goes with Αἴας, whose verb is βεβλήκει, the pluperfect of βάλλω ‘had struck’, with στῆθος ‘on the chest’ and ὑπὲρ ἄντυγος ‘above the rim’ (of Hector’s shield). στρόμβον is a spinning top; ἔσσευε is the imperfect of σεύω ‘set in motion’, and βαλών ‘having struck’. The one who ran round (περὶ δ’ ἔδραμε πάντῃ) can only be Hector, spun by the blow.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ὑπὸ πληγῆς πατρὸς Διὸς ἐξερίπῃ δρῦς
πρόρριζος, δεινὴ δὲ θεείου γίγνεται ὀδμὴ
ἐξ αὐτῆς, τὸν δ’ οὔ περ ἔχει θράσος ὅς κεν ἴδηται
ἐγγὺς ἐών, χαλεπὸς δὲ Διὸς μεγάλοιο κεραυνός,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hoth’ hypo plēgēs patros Dios exeripēi drys
prorrizos, deinē de theeiou gignetai odmē
ex autēs, ton d’ ou per echei thrasos hos ken idētai
engys eōn, chalepos de Dios megaloio keraunos,
sentences.l:
And as when under the blow of father Zeus an oak crashes down
root and all, and a dread smell of sulphur comes
from it, and him courage does not hold, whoever may see it
being near, for harsh is the thunderbolt of great Zeus,
sentences.i: As when an oak crashes down, root and all, beneath the blow of father Zeus, and a dread smell of sulphur rises from it, and courage does not hold the man who sees it close at hand, for harsh is the thunderbolt of great Zeus,
sentences.n: A simile for Hector’s fall; the matching clause is the next unit, which begins ὣς. ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ is ‘and as when’. ἐξερίπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐξερείπω, ‘falls (uprooted)’, with πρόρριζος ‘root and all’. θεείου is the genitive of θέειον ‘sulphur’, and ὀδμή ‘smell’. θράσος is courage (Attic θάρσος), and ὅς κεν ἴδηται ‘whoever sees’ is a general clause.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔπεσ’ Ἕκτορος ὦκα χαμαὶ μένος ἐν κονίῃσι·
sentences.tr: hōs epes’ Hektoros ōka chamai menos en koniēisi·
sentences.l: so fell the might of Hector swiftly to the ground in the dust;
sentences.i: so the might of Hector fell quickly to the ground in the dust;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὡς of the simile. μένος is ‘might’, the fighting strength that is Hector himself, and it ‘falls’ in place of the man. ἔπεσ’ is ἔπεσε, and ὦκα is ‘swiftly’. κονίῃσι is the plural of κονία ‘dust’, a poetic plural, with the epic dative ending -ῃσι.

sentences.t:
χειρὸς δ’ ἔκβαλεν ἔγχος, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ δ’ ἀσπὶς ἑάφθη
καὶ κόρυς, ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ βράχε τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
cheiros d’ ekbalen enchos, ep’ autōi d’ aspis heaphthē
kai korys, amphi de hoi brache teuchea poikila chalkōi.
sentences.l:
and from his hand he cast the spear, and upon him the shield fell
and the helmet, and around him clashed the armour, intricate with bronze.
sentences.i: He let the spear fall from his hand, and the shield and the helmet fell upon him, and his armour, intricate with bronze, clashed around him.
sentences.n: ἔκβαλεν is ‘cast out’, here ‘let fall’, with χειρός ‘from his hand’. ἑάφθη is a rare aorist passive, probably of ἅπτω, with a sense not quite certain; ‘fell’ is the usual guess, and ἐπ’ αὐτῷ means ‘upon him’. βράχε is an unaugmented aorist, ‘clashed’, of a loud ringing sound. τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ is ‘intricate armour with bronze’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ μέγα ἰάχοντες ἐπέδραμον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
ἐλπόμενοι ἐρύεσθαι, ἀκόντιζον δὲ θαμειὰς
αἰχμάς·
sentences.tr:
hoi de mega iachontes epedramon huies Achaiōn
elpomenoi eryesthai, akontizon de thameias
aichmas·
sentences.i: And the sons of the Achaeans ran up shouting loudly, hoping to drag him away, and cast their spears thick and fast;
sentences.n: ἰάχοντες is the participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, and ἐπέδραμον ‘ran up’ is the aorist of ἐπιτρέχω. ἐρύεσθαι is the infinitive of ἐρύω ‘drag’, the verb for hauling a ship; the object, Hector, is understood. ἀκόντιζον is the imperfect of ἀκοντίζω ‘cast a javelin’, and θαμειάς ‘thick, close together’ agrees with αἰχμάς, ‘spear-points’, that is, spears.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ τις ἐδυνήσατο ποιμένα λαῶν
οὐτάσαι οὐδὲ βαλεῖν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ou tis edynēsato poimena laōn
outasai oude balein·
sentences.l:
but no one was able the shepherd of the people
to wound or to strike;
sentences.i: but no one was able to wound or to strike the shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Hector, here in the stock phrase for a leader. ἐδυνήσατο is the aorist of δύναμαι ‘be able’, and οὐτάσαι and βαλεῖν are the aorist infinitives ‘to wound’ and ‘to strike’.

sentences.t:
πρὶν γὰρ περίβησαν ἄριστοι
Πουλυδάμας τε καὶ Αἰνείας καὶ δῖος Ἀγήνωρ
Σαρπηδών τ’ ἀρχὸς Λυκίων καὶ Γλαῦκος ἀμύμων.
sentences.tr:
prin gar peribēsan aristoi
Poulydamas te kai Aineias kai dios Agēnōr
Sarpēdōn t’ archos Lykiōn kai Glaukos amymōn.
sentences.i: for before that the best men had stood over him: Polydamas and Aeneas and heavenly Agenor, and Sarpedon, commander of the Lycians, and blameless Glaucus.
sentences.n: πρίν is ‘before that, sooner’, and περίβησαν is the aorist of περιβαίνω ‘step round’, used of standing over a man to guard him. ἄριστοι ‘the best’ are named in the next lines. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is Agenor’s stock epithet, translated every time in the same way, and so is ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ for Glaucus; its meaning is not known. ἀρχός is ‘commander’, and Πουλυδάμας is Polydamas, in the spelling the edition prints.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὔ τίς εὑ ἀκήδεσεν, ἀλλὰ πάροιθεν
ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους σχέθον αὐτοῦ.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn ou tis heu akēdesen, alla paroithen
aspidas eukyklous schethon autou.
sentences.l:
And of the others none neglected him, but in front
they held their well-rounded shields right there.
sentences.i: And of the others none neglected him, but they held their well-rounded shields in front of him, right there.
sentences.n: τῶν ἄλλων is ‘of the others’, and εὑ is the epic ‘him’ (Hector), the object of ἀκήδεσεν ‘neglected’. πάροιθεν is ‘in front’. σχέθον is the aorist of ἔχω, ‘held’, and εὐκύκλους ‘well-rounded’ is the shield’s epithet. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘right there’, though it could also be read as ‘of him’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἑταῖροι
χερσὶν ἀείραντες φέρον ἐκ πόνου, ὄφρ’ ἵκεθ’ ἵππους
ὠκέας, οἵ οἱ ὄπισθε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο
ἕστασαν ἡνίοχόν τε καὶ ἅρματα ποικίλ’ ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ar’ hetairoi
chersin aeirantes pheron ek ponou, ophr’ hiketh’ hippous
ōkeas, hoi hoi opisthe machēs ēde ptolemoio
hestasan hēniochon te kai harmata poikil’ echontes·
sentences.l:
and him then his companions
with their hands lifting bore out of the toil, until he came to the horses,
swift ones, which for him behind the fight and the war
stood, having charioteer and intricate chariot;
sentences.i: and his companions lifted him in their hands and carried him out of the toil, until he came to the swift horses that stood for him behind the fight and the war, with their charioteer and their intricate chariot;
sentences.n: ἑταῖροι ‘companions’ are the subject, and τὸν ‘him’ is Hector. ἀείραντες ‘lifting’ and φέρον ‘bore’ make one action, and ἐκ πόνου is ‘out of the toil’. ὄφρ’ ἵκεθ’ is ‘until he came’ (ἵκεθ’ = ἵκετο, unaugmented). The horses ὠκέας ‘swift’ ἕστασαν ‘stood’, a pluperfect with past sense, with the charioteer and the chariot, ἅρματα being a plural for one chariot.

sentences.t: οἳ τόν γε προτὶ ἄστυ φέρον βαρέα στενάχοντα.
sentences.tr: hoi ton ge proti asty pheron barea stenachonta.
sentences.l: and they to the city bore him, heavily groaning.
sentences.i: and they carried him to the city, groaning heavily.
sentences.n: οἳ is ‘they’, the companions, and τόν γε is ‘him’, with γε stressing it. προτὶ is the epic form of πρός ‘to’, and ἄστυ ‘city’. βαρέα στενάχοντα is ‘heavily groaning’, the neuter plural βαρέα used as an adverb, and the groaning is Hector’s own. The scene ends with him borne toward Troy.
